concepts.def: Each studied religion grounds belief in sacred texts and authoritative figures - such as the Bible, Qur'an, Torah or Guru Granth Sahib - interpreted within a living tradition.
Conceptions of God or the ultimate differ across traditions, from the Trinity in Christianity and Tawhid in Islam to Brahman in Hinduism and nibbana in Buddhism.
Teachings range from resurrection and judgement in Christianity, Islam and Judaism to rebirth shaped by karma in Hinduism, Buddhism and Sikhism.

Worship, festivals, pilgrimage, dress and diet - such as the Eucharist, salah or the langar kitchen - express belonging and belief in practice.
Each tradition responds to secularism, science, pluralism and changing views of gender, family and authority in the modern world.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Study of Religion: Christianity / Islam / Buddhism / Hinduism / Judaism / Sikhism — a core area of A-Level Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Study of Religion: Christianity / Islam / Buddhism / Hinduism / Judaism / Sikhism brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Study of Religion: Christianity / Islam / Buddhism / Hinduism / Judaism / Sikhism.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What does the Study of Religion component require of your chosen religion?
options: Examining its sources of authority, view of ultimate reality, beliefs about death, moral principles and expressions of identity
Studying only its festivals
Covering all six religions in equal depth in one exam
Studying only its history before 1500

mcqs.q: Which pairing of religion and scripture is correct?
options: Sikhism - the Guru Granth Sahib
Islam - the Vedas
Buddhism - the Torah
Hinduism - the Qur'an

mcqs.q: Which term describes the oneness of God in Islam?
options: Tawhid
Trinity
Brahman
Anatta

mcqs.q: Beliefs about 'self, death and afterlife' in Hinduism centre on what?
options: Reincarnation of the atman according to karma until liberation (moksha)
Bodily resurrection on a final day of judgement
The complete end of existence at death with no continuity
Ancestors becoming household gods automatically

mcqs.q: Are all religions basically the same underneath?
options: The six religions share a single founder.
Scriptures are only read by clergy, never by ordinary believers.

No - there are real overlaps, such as compassion and charity, but core claims differ sharply: theism versus non-theism, resurrection versus rebirth; precise study requires the specific tradition's own terms.
All six religions teach the same things with different names.

mcqs.q: Do all believers read their scriptures in the same way?
options: Scriptures are only read by clergy, never by ordinary believers.
The six religions share a single founder.
No - every tradition contains literal, contextual and allegorical approaches, and internal diversity between denominations and schools is itself part of what you study.
Each religion has one official way of reading its scripture that all members accept.

mcqs.q: Is religious authority only a matter of holy books?
options: Religious authority is decided by national governments.
Scripture is the only source of authority in any religion.
Scriptures are only read by clergy, never by ordinary believers.
No - authority also flows through community tradition, leaders and teachers, conscience, reason and religious experience, and traditions weigh these differently.

sequence.def: Vedas composed from c.1500 BC, the oldest living tradition
Mosaic covenant at Sinai, traditionally c.1300 BC
The Buddha teaches in India, c.5th century BC
Begins with Jesus's ministry, 1st century AD
Hijrah of Muhammad to Madinah, 622 AD
Founded by Guru Nanak, born 1469 AD
